items.body_md:
On August 17, Judge P. Kevin Castel signed the memo endorsement at Dkt. 94 in *Hachette Book Group, Inc. et al. v. Meta Platforms, Inc.*, No. 1:26-cv-03689 (S.D.N.Y.), terminating Samuel Rubinstein as counsel of record for all plaintiffs. The withdrawal is procedural and, on its face, routine — Rubinstein's motion (Dkt. 93, filed August 14) was unopposed and the memo endorsement disposed of it the same day it was entered on the docket. The client roster and the substantive posture are unchanged. What the withdrawal does not resolve, and what continues to ripen toward the September 15 initial conference before Judge Castel (Courtroom 11D, 3:00 PM), is the live dispute over plaintiffs' letter motion for leave to file a motion to strike (Dkt. 90, August 3) and Meta's responsive letter (Dkt. 92, August 7). Judge Castel has not yet authorized briefing on the motion-to-strike question; the September 15 conference is the next event where that authorization — and any direction on Google's transfer motion analogue in the related Gemini action — may materially advance both dockets simultaneously.

Also on August 17, Meta filed exhibits at Dkt. 810 in *Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc.*, No. 3:23-cv-03417 (N.D. Cal., Chhabria, J.), in compliance with the sealing order at Dkt. 805 governing materials submitted in connection with Dkt. 781. Six exhibit attachments were filed — Exhibits B, D, E, F, G, and H — by Phillip Morton. The filing is substantive in classification (it executes a court order on the scope of sealed materials related to prior merits briefing), but routine in the sense that it resolves no independently contested issue; it completes the public-record compliance exercise Chhabria directed and has no independent bearing on the contributory infringement amendment posture or the coordinated deposition schedule. The further case management conference docketed August 17 — listed without an attached minute entry in the RECAP record, consistent with 
CourtListener's last-updated timestamp of August 14, 2026, at 11:21 AM and last known filing date of August 13, 2026
 — means the August 17 CMC entry itself has not yet generated a public minute entry confirming what Chhabria directed. That minute entry, once posted, governs the deposition-sequencing and class certification / summary judgment coordination that the August 14 conference addressed, including the confirmed 4-hour cap on Mark Zuckerberg's deposition and the extension of the Rule 30(b)(6) deposition from 14 to 21 hours. The contributory infringement amendment — 
grounded in the allegation that when Meta downloaded copyrighted works from shadow libraries using BitTorrent, it simultaneously uploaded those works onto the torrenting network, enabling other network members to infringe plaintiffs' rights
 — remains the live pleading question pending further direction from Chhabria; the August 26 deadline for calendaring Zuckerberg's deposition in the related *Entrepreneur Media, LLC v. Meta Platforms, Inc.*, No. 3:25-cv-09579 (N.D. Cal.), is the nearest time-sensitive marker across the Chhabria cluster.

*Getty Images (US), Inc. v. Stability AI, Inc. et al.*, No. 3:25-cv-06891 (N.D. Cal., Thompson, J.), *Encyclopaedia Britannica, Inc. and Merriam-Webster, Inc. v. OpenAI, Inc. et al.*, No. 1:26-cv-02097 (S.D.N.Y., Stein, J.), *Hachette v. Google (Gemini)*, No. 1:26-cv-05870 (S.D.N.Y., Preska, J.), and *Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH et al. v. Ross Intelligence, Inc.*, No. 25-2153 (3d Cir.), recorded no docket movement. In the Getty action, the scheduling-modification dispute is fully submitted before Judge Thompson following the August 17 responses-due deadline; a ruling — granting or denying both Getty's leave motion (Dkt. 70) and the underlying request to modify the scheduling order (Dkt. 68) — remains the next concrete milestone there. In the Google Gemini action, the transfer motion remains under submission before Judge Preska. In the Third Circuit, the panel of Judges Restrepo, Montgomery-Reeves, and Bove continues to deliberate following the June 11 oral argument.

items.lede: On August 17, the publishers filed their Responsive Separate Statement (Dkt. 756) together with a supporting declaration (Dkt. 757), a notice (Dkt. 758), and two documents under seal (Dkts. 759–760), completing the publishers' opposition-side factual record on the cross-motions for summary judgment before Judge Eumi K. items.body_md:
On August 17, the publishers filed their Responsive Separate Statement (Dkt. 756) together with a supporting declaration (Dkt. 757), a notice (Dkt. 758), and two documents under seal (Dkts. 759–760), completing the publishers' opposition-side factual record on the cross-motions for summary judgment before Judge Eumi K. Lee in No. 5:24-cv-03811. The Responsive Separate Statement is the publishers' point-by-point answer to Anthropic's separate statement of undisputed facts — the document that locks in which material facts the publishers dispute, on what evidentiary basis, and where genuine issues of fact exist that the court must resolve before it can grant or deny either side's motion. Because the summary judgment hearing is set for October 21, this filing completes the factual-dispute record that Judge Lee will have in front of her; it is not a preliminary skirmish.

The sealed companion filings (Dkts. 759–760) almost certainly carry the underlying exhibits the declaration references — consistent with the pattern set by the July 27 round of sealed Daubert oppositions (Dkts. 745–753), where substantive evidence was filed under the standing sealing order (Dkt. 590). The content is not publicly available, but the structure of the filing cluster mirrors prior sealed merits submissions in this case. What matters for recovery posture is the scope of what the publishers chose to contest: a narrow responsive statement, accepting most of Anthropic's facts, would signal confidence that disputed facts alone carry their partial summary judgment motion on direct infringement; a broad one, contesting the bulk of Anthropic's statement, signals that the publishers view the factual record as genuinely contested on fair use and may be laying the foundation for a trial rather than a clean pre-trial adjudication. That distinction cannot be assessed until the sealed exhibits surface or the court rules.


The publishers have narrowed Concord I to direct infringement and alleged removal of copyright management information, having dropped earlier contributory and vicarious infringement claims.
 The summary judgment motion accordingly turns on whether Anthropic's training use was fair use — 
Anthropic argues the use was "transformative" fair use analogous to how humans learn from reading, while the publishers counter that Anthropic used the lyrics to build a competing commercial product and fair use does not apply.
 Running in parallel, 
Anthropic and Dario Amodei have each filed dismissal motions in Concord II targeting the case covering more than 20,000 songs, with Anthropic seeking to strike the output-reproduction claim and a DMCA count.
 The November 4 hearing on those partial motions to dismiss in No. 5:26-cv-00880 is the next inflection point for the broader multi-suit exposure picture. The next concrete milestone in Concord I is the September 2 Case Management Conference before Judge Lee, followed by the October 21 summary judgment hearing.

items.body_md:
On August 17, the Harvest Sherwood docket recorded two claim assignments (Dkts. 1217–1218), a compensation filing (Dkt. 1220), a generic notice (Dkt. 1223), and three pro hac vice admissions (Dkts. 1219, 1221–1222) — the last category procedural and routine. The two claim assignments continue the secondary-market trading pattern running through this case since at least early August; at the dollar levels typical of this estate (trade claims in the $200–$400 million range), they are substantive but routine, consistent with the prior transfers documented in Dkt. 1165 and the August 13–14 run. Dkt. 1220, styled "Compensation AND Compensation," most likely reflects a fee application or interim compensation order; without confirmed document text it is treated as substantive-but-routine and earns no further weight here.

The more consequential development post-dates the prior briefing by several weeks and is not yet reflected in the docket record as presented. 
Sprouts Farmers Market's Q2 2026 Form 10-Q, filed with the SEC on July 29, 2026, discloses that in June 2026 the parties agreed in principle to settle all pending litigation and release all claims against each other in exchange for payment of an amount Sprouts characterizes as immaterial, and that the settlement was approved by the Bankruptcy Court on July 27, 2026, subject to a seven-day appeal period.
 The approval order — almost certainly a 9019 order entered by Judge Jernigan — would be the operative confirmation event on the Harvest Sherwood docket, but that entry is not visible in the docket record provided here. The settlement approval should appear as a signed order in Adv. Pro. 25-08002; that is the primary source that would confirm finality, and it should be retrieved from PACER to verify whether any timely appeal was filed within the seven-day window following July 27. The September 21, 2026 trial date and deadline remaining in the case management system are almost certainly superseded entries that predate the settlement order; they should be treated as stale absent contrary evidence from the adversary proceeding docket.

The recovery implication for unsecured creditors is material and adverse relative to the pre-settlement posture. 
The adversary proceeding had sought $41.8 million plus punitive damages from Sprouts, asserting fraudulent transfer, breach of contract, fraud, and unjust enrichment.
 
Sprouts had counterclaimed for approximately $65.0 million, asserting breach of contract, negligent misrepresentation, and unjust enrichment.
 Sprouts' own 10-Q characterizes the settlement payment as immaterial — a formulation that, in public-company disclosure practice, typically means below the threshold of financial significance for a company of Sprouts' scale — which signals a recovery well below the $41.8 million headline demand, and almost certainly a fraction of it. The elimination of Sprouts' $65 million counterclaim exposure is a corresponding benefit to the estate, but it is a defensive gain, not a recovery. With Adv. Pro. 25-08002 resolved, 
the primary remaining litigation asset is prosecution of antitrust claims against over 25 defendants, collection of remaining accounts receivable, and administration of settlement proceeds
 — and 
with $44.6 million in antitrust settlements already achieved against estimated $1.09 billion in claims across 28-plus defendants, additional recoveries remain pending.
 The next concrete milestone for creditor recovery is the continued prosecution and resolution of those antitrust claims; there is no remaining docket deadline in Adv. Pro. 25-08002 that warrants monitoring.

items.body_md:
On August 17, an appellee filed the counter-designation of record on appeal (Dkt. 374), completing the record-designation phase under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8009. The filing lands 14 days after Samara CR Holdings, LLC and Jason M. Kahan served their Statement of Issues and Designation of Record (Dkt. 357, filed August 3), placing it precisely at the outer edge of the appellee's counter-designation window under Rule 8009(a)(2). The appellee — most likely Trustee Donald Lassman or PBTC Recovery Partners, LLC, or both — has now put additional record items on the table to supplement what the appellants designated, a standard tool for a winning party to ensure the appellate court sees the full record context, not just the slice the appellants chose.

The practical consequence is that record designation is now closed on both sides. The bankruptcy court clerk can certify and transmit the complete record to the district court, which starts the 30-day opening-brief clock under Fed. R. Bankr. P. 8018(a)(1). Given the transcript-filing activity earlier this month, transmission could come within days. Until the district court dockets the transmitted record, the briefing schedule remains unset; creditors and parties tracking recovery should watch for that docketing event, which will fix the deadline by which Samara and Kahan must file the opening brief pressing their four issues — the due-process/hearing-expansion challenge, the § 363(m) good-faith finding for PBTC, the Howard Jahre conflict-of-interest argument, and the propriety of vacating the July 2 order on oral motion.

Dkts. 372 and 373, if docketed between August 15 and August 16, have not been flagged as moved in the materials available; the next concrete milestone is the district court's docketing of the transmitted appellate record, which sets the opening-brief deadline.

items.body_md:
On August 17, Omnis Fuel Technologies, LLC and Quantum Pleasants, LLC served the debtor with a First Set of Requests for Production (Dkt. 99), filed by Christopher Ward of Lowenstein Sandler LLP — the same firm that secured pro hac vice admission for Michael A. Kaplan and Rebecca J. Ryan on the same date (Dkts. 95–98). The RFP service is the first formal discovery move in the case and is substantively important in context: Lowenstein Sandler's entry, concurrent with the dismissal motion filed August 14 (Dkt. 93), signals that Omnis Fuel Technologies and Quantum Pleasants are building a litigation record in support of their bad-faith/no-authority theory, not merely pressing a pleading. Discovery directed at the debtor in connection with a dismissal motion is irregular — such motions are typically decided on the pleadings and existing record — and its issuance suggests the movants either anticipate an evidentiary hearing before Judge Owens or are laying groundwork for one by forcing document production before the August 28 objection deadline on Dkt. 93. Dkts. 95–98 (the pro hac vice motions and orders for Kaplan and Ryan) are procedural and routine.

The practical effect for the debtor is immediate: a discovery obligation now runs in parallel with its obligation to file an objection to the dismissal/trustee motion by August 28. The debtor will need to decide whether to move for a protective order or comply, and any delay in the sale marketing process attributable to discovery litigation could compress Houlihan Lokey's runway before the September 3 final cash collateral hearing. For creditors — particularly the West Virginia Economic Development Authority, holding an unsecured claim of approximately $50.9 million — the introduction of formal discovery into what was nominally a dismissal motion raises the stakes of that hearing materially. If the movants use the RFP responses to sharpen the evidentiary case for bad faith, the debtor's opposition will need to be more than a legal brief: it will need to address factual record developed from its own documents. The alternative interpretation — that the RFP is tactical pressure rather than a genuine evidentiary project — is also plausible, but the simultaneous admission of two Lowenstein Sandler partners with specialized litigation backgrounds is more consistent with a coordinated discovery-and-briefing strategy than with a motion the movants expect to win on the papers alone.

Tomorrow, August 19, is the objection deadline on the prepetition taxes and fees interim order (Dkt. 49, capped at $775,000). No objections have appeared on the docket as of today; if none are filed by 4:00 p.m. Eastern, the court may enter the final order without a further hearing. The next hard deadline after that is August 27 (objections to the five professional retention applications, Dkts. 81–85), followed by August 28 (objections to the dismissal/trustee motion, Dkt. 93), with the September 3 final hearings on cash collateral, first-day orders, and professional retentions — and the Section 341 meeting of creditors on September 2 — constituting the case's next inflection cluster.

items.body_md:
On August 17, Papaya Gaming's counsel filed a Certification of Counsel (Dkt. 69) in Case No. 26-11217 before Judge Mary F. Walrath, U.S. Bankruptcy Court, D. Delaware. A Certification of Counsel is the standard Delaware bankruptcy mechanism by which a party certifies that no objection has been received — or that all parties have agreed on form — and submits a proposed order directly to the judge for entry without a hearing. The underlying subject matter of the proposed order is not disclosed on the face of the docket entry, and the full text of Dkt. 69 is not available in the public record accessed for this briefing; the content and significance of the order it seeks remain unverified until either the document itself or the court's response order appears on the docket. What is clear is that a proposed order is now sitting with Judge Walrath awaiting entry, and the matter was sufficiently uncontested — or resolved among the parties — to proceed by certification rather than noticed motion. If the proposed order relates to scheduling the recognition hearing or to the scope of the temporary injunction (the two live substantive threads on this docket), it would carry material consequence for Skillz/Firy's collection timeline; if it is administrative in nature, it carries none. Confirmation requires the court's responsive order, which should appear on the docket within days of the certification.

The active substantive posture is otherwise unchanged: 
Judge Walrath's temporary injunction stays collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets, preserving the status quo pending a hearing on Papaya's petition for formal recognition under Chapter 15
, and 
that relief was granted despite strong opposition from Skillz, now operating as Firy Inc.
 The deposition notices filed August 11 (Dkts. 61–62) remain the clearest signal that both sides are building evidentiary records for the recognition hearing rather than standing down. 
Judge Cote's underlying judgment requires Papaya to pay approximately $719 million in disgorgement, as well as approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and legal costs
 — the full amount blocked from collection while the temporary injunction holds. For Skillz/Firy, a denial of recognition remains the path to enforcement; 
if the Delaware bankruptcy court approves the petition, Skillz would be blocked from collecting on the $719 million judgment while Papaya's appeal plays out.


The next concrete milestone is the court's entry of whatever order Dkt. 69 proposes — likely within the next two to five business days, absent judicial hold. If that order sets or confirms the recognition hearing date, it becomes the governing milestone for the stay's duration and creditor recovery timing.

items.body_md:
On August 17, Judge O'Hagan entered an interim order and set a final hearing (Dkt. 138), filed in conjunction with a new motion to shorten time (Dkt. 137) and a Text Order — the trio signaling that at least one pending matter was resolved on an interim basis and placed on an accelerated final-hearing track.

The docket label for Dkt. 138 — "Interim Order – Final Hearing" — is the standard D.N.J. designation for a court-entered interim relief order that reserves final determination for a noticed hearing. Given that the August 14 9019 settlement motion (Dkt. 129) and its companion shorten-time motion (Dkt. 130) have been on the docket for three days without a publicly visible ruling, and that a new shorten-time motion (Dkt. 137) and a new generic motion (Dkt. 139) also landed August 17, the interim order most plausibly resolves one of those pending matters — but the docket entries alone do not identify the subject motion with certainty, and no secondary reporting has confirmed the content of Dkt. 138. What can be stated on the docket record: Judge O'Hagan acted, interim relief issued, and a final hearing has been calendared. The corresponding Hearing Scheduled entry (Dkt. 142) records the clerk's notice of that final hearing date, which is not yet visible from the publicly provided docket data. If Dkt. 138 touches the 9019 settlement (Dkt. 129), any interim relief on that motion would constitute a substantive development for creditors — settlement terms affecting asset title, lien priority, or claim allowance directly shape what is available to the estate ahead of the September 8 bid deadline. If Dkt. 138 instead resolves a retention or first-day administrative matter, its impact on recovery is marginal unless the terms were contested.

Also filed August 17: Dkt. 140, an amended motion combined with a retention application, which mirrors the August 14 Dkt. 127 filing in form. Absent evidence of a contested objection, retention filings are procedural and routine; Dkt. 140 carries no independent weight on recovery unless the U.S. Trustee or a creditor body challenges it. Dkt. 139, styled as a generic motion, has no secondary reporting and its subject matter is unverified — classify up until the document is available. Dkts. 131–136 are BNC certificates of notice, procedural filing infrastructure with no bearing on recovery or timing.

The 9019 settlement motion (Dkt. 129) and the trustee motion (Dkt. 103, filed by creditor Lin Liang) both remain unresolved on the public record. The trustee motion turns on whether the debtors' principal misappropriated customer funds, a question that retains independent force even in a liquidating case — an appointed trustee displaces the CRO and changes the investigative posture of the estate entirely. The next concrete milestones are September 8 (qualified bid deadline for the West Texas auction) and September 10 (auction for the Pyote and Tarbush sites). Any matter touching lien status, claim allowance, or estate control needs to clear before those dates; the interim order entered at Dkt. 138 and the final hearing it schedules will bear watching on that timeline.

items.body_md:
On August 14, InvestmentNews published additional detail from the SEC complaint that adds a discrete fraud-on-investors allegation not foregrounded in the August 11 agency press releases. 
After distributions halted in November 2025, Delgado emailed investors blaming a "third-party audit" and "additional compliance and forensic accounting requirements" for the delays; the SEC alleges those explanations were false and designed "to lull investors and conceal Defendants' fraud."
 That allegation matters for recovery posture because it extends the actionable misconduct timeline beyond the operational scheme itself into the wind-down period — potential fodder for a separate fraudulent-concealment or equitable-tolling argument by claimants whose limitations clock might otherwise start running earlier. 
A court-appointed receiver later steered Goliath into the bankruptcy now pending before Judge Mark.
 The InvestmentNews piece adds no new primary-source filings; it is secondary reporting drawing on the face of the SEC complaint.

The InvestmentNews piece also surfaces one granular allegation from the SEC complaint that rounds out the misappropriation picture: 
the SEC alleges Delgado personally misappropriated at least $51 million and that defendants misused roughly $281 million more to sustain promised distributions flowing to earlier investors.
 That $281 million figure — the Ponzi-payment tranche — is distinct from both the sales-commission flows alleged in the CFTC complaint and from Delgado's personal extraction, and it represents the largest single category of alleged misuse. For unsecured creditors, the practical implication is that the recoverable asset pool is bounded not by the gross intake but by what remains after those three drains; the DOJ's civil forfeiture complaint, which targets seven real properties and eleven vehicles, represents one concrete slice of the personal-extraction tranche. 
The United States filed a civil forfeiture complaint against seven real properties and eleven vehicles allegedly purchased with fraud proceeds, alleging approximately $17 million in victim funds went to homes and office space and more than $2.5 million to purchase, lease, or pay off loans on the vehicles.


No new docket entries have been identified in Case No. 26-13174-RAM since the August 13 briefing. The materiality picture is unchanged: the September 30, 2026 proof-of-claim bar date in Case No. 26-13174-RAM remains the most immediate hard deadline for claimants on notice from the SEC and CFTC enforcement releases. 
The DOJ's case page lists Delgado's criminal sentencing for October 21, 2026, with the criminal investigation described as still ongoing
 — that date, rather than the October 8 entry in the docket record, is what the DOJ's own page reflects; the discrepancy between the two dates should be tracked, as the sentencing hearing is the event at which restitution and forfeiture amounts will be set and which will directly shape the asset pool available to the estate.

items.body_md:
On August 14, a motion to employ attorney was filed at Dkt. 535, alongside a notice of change of address at Dkt. 536. The employment motion is the only entry from the lookback period that warrants analysis — the change-of-address notice is procedural and routine. The identity of the attorney sought to be employed and the proposed scope of representation are not evident from the docket entry alone; the full text of Dkt. 535 is not available from the record provided. Retention applications are ordinarily procedural and routine, but a new attorney engagement at this stage carries at least some substantive relevance: the case is deep into a contested Chapter 11 with an active adversary proceeding (Adv. No. 26-02122, filed June 24 against Coinbase Global, Coinbase Inc., Coinbase Financial Markets, Aaron Tilton, and Brad Jones, for recovery of money and property), and who is being retained — and in what capacity — determines whether Dkt. 535 is an estate-value question or administrative housekeeping. Until the application's content can be confirmed from PACER, Dkt. 535 should be treated as potentially significant and monitored for any objection or opposition, which would elevate it to substantive-and-important territory.

The broader posture gives that monitoring urgency. 
The case carries over $192 million in total claims, including Celsius Network LLC claims exceeding $133 million.
 Earlier this month, Brian Rothschild — counsel for the debtor — was moving party on the motion to liquidate certain assets held in the debtor's B2C2 account (Dkt. 472), a hearing on which was calendared for August 11. No order resolving that motion appears on the docket record provided, meaning its disposition remains an open recovery question. Any new attorney engagement touching estate litigation — including the Coinbase adversary — would be substantive, not administrative.

Dkt. 536 (notice of change of address) is procedural and routine; it earns no further analysis. The next concrete milestone to track is the outcome of the B2C2 liquidation motion (Dkt. 472), for which no order has yet appeared, and the filing of any objection to the Dkt. 535 retention application, with a response deadline that will run from service of that motion.

items.body_md:
On August 11, the CIT entered an order scheduling a closed settlement conference for August 25, 2026 at 2:00 p.m. EDT in *V.O.S. Selections, Inc. v. United States* (No. 25-00066), consolidating it with the parallel *Freestyle World, Inc. v. United States* (No. 26-01088) proceeding before the same bench. __[CourtListener — V.O.S. Selections CIT Docket](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/69888953/vos-selections-inc-v-trump/)__ The August 25 conference follows directly on oral argument held August 6 on the competing Rule 23(b)(2) class certification motions in both cases — the transcript of that argument was filed August 12, with a notice-of-intent-to-redact deadline of August 19. No ruling on certification has issued.

The August 25 conference is the pivot point the market is watching. 
A closed settlement conference was held on August 5 — if those discussions bear fruit, a negotiated resolution could bypass the litigation tracks entirely.
 __[Troutman Pepper Locke, Aug. 13, 2026](https://www.troutman.com/insights/to-sue-or-not-to-sue-that-is-the-question-for-ieepa-tariff-refunds/)__ The August 25 session extends that dynamic, pulling both the *V.O.S.* and *Freestyle World* parties into the same room. What the court is testing is whether a negotiated expansion of CAPE eligibility — covering finally-liquidated entries held by importers who never filed suit — can be structured without requiring a class certification ruling or surviving the DOJ's pending Federal Circuit appeal of the CIT's universal refund order. 
The appeal targets the order's application to finally liquidated entries for importers who never filed suit at the CIT, arguing the CIT's order amounts to an impermissible universal injunction, and the government has indicated it may seek to retain an estimated $30 billion or more in IEEPA tariffs collected on those entries if its position prevails.
 __[The Tariff Bureau](https://tariffbureau.com/updates)__

The class certification question frames the settlement's stakes precisely. 
The *V.O.S.* plaintiffs filed their Rule 23(b)(2) motion on June 4, 2026, seeking certification on behalf of all importers whose IEEPA refund claims remain ineligible for processing through CAPE; if granted, the certification would include every such importer and could compel the government to open CAPE to the entire class.
 __[Troutman Pepper Locke, July 6, 2026](https://www.troutman.com/insights/beyond-cape-importers-move-for-class-certification-to-recover-liquidated-ieepa-tariffs-not-covered-in-phase-1-of-refund-process/)__ 
After Euro-Notions Florida, Inc. voluntarily dismissed its case, Judge Eaton designated *Freestyle World* (CIT No. 26-01088) as the new lead case for the consolidated IEEPA refund litigation, and the selection of *Freestyle World* — which has its own pending class certification motion — may signal the court's inclination toward addressing the refund gap through class-action mechanisms.
 __[Troutman Pepper Locke, Aug. 13, 2026](https://www.troutman.com/insights/to-sue-or-not-to-sue-that-is-the-question-for-ieepa-tariff-refunds/)__ 
A certified class is legally distinct from a universal injunction: class members are, by definition, parties to the case, so relief granted to a class would not violate any prohibition on orders benefiting nonparties — meaning class certification could serve as a legal workaround for whatever limitations the Federal Circuit imposes on the CIT's injunctive power.
 __[Troutman Pepper Locke, Aug. 13, 2026](https://www.troutman.com/insights/to-sue-or-not-to-sue-that-is-the-question-for-ieepa-tariff-refunds/)__

The Federal Circuit briefing schedule on the government's appeal of the refund order adds time pressure to both tracks. 
The government's opening brief was due August 3, 2026; plaintiffs may submit a response in support by August 14, and oral argument is scheduled for August 19, 2026.
 __[Troutman Pepper Locke, Aug. 13, 2026](https://www.troutman.com/insights/to-sue-or-not-to-sue-that-is-the-question-for-ieepa-tariff-refunds/)__ That argument lands six days before the August 25 settlement conference — compressing the timeline considerably and giving the Federal Circuit's signals on the universal-injunction question real leverage over what the parties are willing to accept in a negotiated resolution. 
CBP has stated it lacks statutory authority to reliquidate entries outside the 90-day post-liquidation voluntary reliquidation window, and that CAPE Phase 3 programming for finally-liquidated entries will be available only to importers that have filed a CIT action; a CIT ruling on certification is expected shortly but will almost certainly be appealed to the Federal Circuit, and final judicial resolution may not occur before the end of 2026.
 __[BDO, Aug. 10, 2026](https://www.bdo.com/insights/tax/ieepa-tariff-refunds-frequently-asked-questions)__ 
CBP's August 4 progress report made no mention of any pathway for nonlitigant importers, and the next CBP progress report is not due until August 25 — the same date as the settlement conference; given the running of limitations periods, importers with substantial outstanding IEEPA refunds should evaluate whether filing a protective action at the CIT is warranted before deadlines expire.
 __[Troutman Pepper Locke, Aug. 13, 2026](https://www.troutman.com/insights/to-sue-or-not-to-sue-that-is-the-question-for-ieepa-tariff-refunds/)__

*Burlap and Barrel* (CAFC No. 1:26-cv-01606, Judge Stanceu) — where the Federal Circuit's June 11 stay pending appeal (Dkt. 51) remains in effect — is directly downstream of the Federal Circuit's August 19 argument on the government's universal-injunction challenge: the merits panel assigned to *Burlap* will be reading the same briefs and watching the same oral argument before setting its own briefing schedule.

The next concrete milestone is Federal Circuit oral argument, August 19, 2026, in the government's appeal of the CIT's IEEPA refund order — followed immediately by the August 25 closed settlement conference in *V.O.S.* and *Freestyle World* and CBP's next required progress report, also due August 25.

items.lede: On August 12, at least two parties filed oppositions (Dkts. 51 and 52) and one filed an objection (Dkt. 56) against what the docket labels confirm are distinct contested matters, accompanied by a supporting declaration (Dkt. 53) and a stipulation (Dkt. 57) — the heaviest single day of adversarial activity in this case since the first-day hearing.
items.body_md:
On August 12, at least two parties filed oppositions (Dkts. 51 and 52) and one filed an objection (Dkt. 56) against what the docket labels confirm are distinct contested matters, accompanied by a supporting declaration (Dkt. 53) and a stipulation (Dkt. 57) — the heaviest single day of adversarial activity in this case since the first-day hearing. The docket does not yet identify the targets of those filings by description in the materials available to this desk, but the case context narrows the candidates sharply. The CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43, filed August 5) carried an opposition deadline of August 19 and sought court authorization for insider-adjacent compensation — the CRO, Leslie Gladstone, being named in Dkt. 43's attachments — making it a live target for the U.S. Trustee or judgment creditors. The Manatt employment application (Dkt. 42, filed August 5) is the other obvious target; contested retention applications, particularly where the estate is essentially a litigation-liability vehicle funded by a CEO-owned DIP lender, attract U.S. Trustee scrutiny on disinterestedness and connections. The employment application at Dkt. 49 (filed August 10) is too recent to have drawn a deadline-compliant response by August 12 under standard notice periods. Until the full text of Dkts. 51, 52, 53, 56, and 57 is reviewed on PACER, their precise targets remain unverified; the desk flags this and will confirm at next update. What is clear from the docket structure — two oppositions plus a supporting declaration filed the same day as a separate objection — is that at least two distinct contested matters were briefed simultaneously on August 12, a pattern inconsistent with ordinary course and consistent with coordinated creditor or U.S. Trustee opposition.

The Errors/Deficiencies notice at Dkt. 59 (BNC, August 13) and the Generic Order at Dkt. 60 (August 13) are almost certainly related: the deficiency notice identifies a filing that failed to meet local-rule requirements, and the generic order likely resolves or memorializes the correction. This is procedural and carries no independent weight on recovery, though a deficiency on a retention or compensation filing could slow the authorization clock. Dkts. 54 and 55 are certificates of service, and Dkt. 58 is a proof of service (CSD 3010); all three are filing infrastructure and are omitted. The stipulation at Dkt. 57 is substantive in classification — stipulations in contested Chapter 11 matters affect legal rights — but its substance is unverified; if it reflects an agreed resolution of one of the contested matters briefed the same day, it is material to recovery posture, and the desk will confirm.

The contested posture on these professional-retention and compensation matters matters for creditors beyond the immediate cost. 
The two principal judgments — approximately $245 million in the De la Torre class action and approximately $157 million in the CFPB tribal-lending action — together with roughly $45 million in additional pending litigation and about $5 million in trade debt and professional fees, constitute substantially all of the debtor's prepetition obligations
, against reported assets of $1 million to $10 million. In that context, professional fees and CRO compensation drawn from the estate — funded by a ~$4 million DIP facility 
owned by the debtor's CEO
 — are not administrative minutiae; they directly compress whatever is available to unsecured creditors. Vigorous opposition to these applications signals that at least one party is treating the fee burn as a recovery issue, not a routine creditor courtesy. The next concrete milestone is the August 19 opposition deadline on the CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43), which will either close the briefing on that motion or extend it if further responses arrive — and, depending on the scope of Dkt. 56's objection, the court may consolidate argument on the professional matters at a single hearing.
